## Why are we doing this?

An AI can install software, add up numbers
and write proofs faster than either of us ever will.
So why learn any of it?

For the same reason people learned pure math
long before anyone needed it.
Almost nobody uses calculus at work.
What it built was the ability to understand:
to follow an argument, see why it holds,
and notice when it doesn't.

That's the point of this course:
not to get the computer to do things,
but to **understand what it did, and why**,
well enough to catch it when it's wrong.

Every step comes with three habits:

- **Predict.** Before you press Enter, say what will happen.
- **Check.** Did it? If not, that's the interesting part.
- **Explain.** Say *why*, in your own words.

Today, in four parts:

1. **Set up** Linux inside Windows, with an AI tutor beside it.
2. **Python basics:** boxes, questions and repeats.
3. **Add up** 1 to 100, and ask when checking becomes proving.
4. **Lean:** the same program in a language that checks proofs.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to use this page
Each grey box has a copy button in its top right corner.
Paste into the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V and press Enter.
Read the sentence above each box *before* you run it.
:::

# Part 1: Set up

## Turn on Linux (WSL)

Underneath the windows and buttons,
a computer works with text.
A **terminal** is a window where you talk to it in words.
We'll use **Linux**, running inside Windows
(that's **WSL**, Windows Subsystem for Linux).

1. Click Start and type **PowerShell**.
2. Right-click **Windows PowerShell**,
   choose **Run as administrator**, and click Yes.
3. Paste this and press Enter:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

When it says so, **restart the computer**.
A window called **Ubuntu** (our kind of Linux) then opens
and asks you to make up a **username**
(short, lowercase, no spaces) and a **password**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The password is invisible
When you type it, *nothing appears*, not even dots.
That's normal. Type it anyway and press Enter.
:::

From now on, open **Terminal** from the Start menu
and pick **Ubuntu** from the ▾ menu next to the tabs.

## Look around

The line ending in `$` is the **prompt**:
the computer waiting for you.

```bash
pwd
```

`pwd` prints where you are, something like `/home/anna`:
your **home folder**, written as a **path**
(folders inside folders, separated by `/`).

```bash
mkdir course
cd course
pwd
```

**Predict** before the last line: what will `pwd` print now?
(`mkdir` makes a folder, `cd` goes into one,
`cd ..` goes up a level.)

## Stop the password questions

Commands starting with `sudo` run as the administrator,
and Linux asks for your password each time.
The Windows login already protects this computer,
so we tell Linux to stop asking:

```bash
echo "$USER ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/$USER
sudo chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/$USER
```

## Your tutor: Claude Code

**Claude** is an AI, a **language model**:
it learned from a huge amount of text
to predict what words come next.
That turns out to be enough to explain things and write code.
It also makes Claude *very good at sounding right*.
Usually it is right. Sometimes it isn't,
and it can't always tell. That's why you check.

**Claude Code** lets you talk to Claude in the terminal.
You'll need a Claude account.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
```

`curl` downloads the installer, and `| bash` runs it
(the `|`, a *pipe*, sends one command's output into the next).

Claude could do this whole lesson by itself.
That's why we tell it not to.
This box writes a file called `CLAUDE.md`:
standing instructions Claude reads every time it starts in this folder.

```bash
cat > ~/course/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
# Tutor mode

I'm a beginner learning to program, and above all to reason.
The point is that I work things out myself.
You're my tutor, not the one doing the work.

- Never write the code for my exercises,
  and don't run commands or edit files for me.
  If you solve it, the lesson is lost.
- If I paste an error message, explain in plain words
  what it means and where to look. One hint, not the fix.
- If I ask what a command does, explain it simply,
  then ask me to predict what will happen before I run it.
- Ask me "why?" often, and look for the hole
  in my explanations.
- If I ask how you work, or why AI gets things wrong,
  explain honestly and simply. That's part of the course.
- Allowed: if I ask for code *to referee*
  (with a hidden bug for me to find), write it.
- Keep answers short. Use everyday words.
EOF
```

Press **Alt+Shift+D** to split the window into two panes.
In the **right** pane, start Claude:

```bash
cd ~/course
claude
```

The first time, it opens a browser to log in.
Claude asks before it does anything on your computer:
say no unless you understand what it's asking.

Try two questions:
*"What did the `cat > CLAUDE.md` command I just ran do?"*
and *"When are you most likely to be wrong?"*

From now on:
**left pane, you work. Right pane, you ask.**

::: {.callout-tip}
## Asking well
Claude only knows what you tell it.
A good question says **what you did**, **what happened**,
and **what you think**:
*"I ran `python3 gauss.py` and got this error: (paste).
I think line 3 is wrong. Am I right?"*
Errors are normal. Read each one yourself first and guess,
then paste it with your guess. Fixing it is your job.
:::

## A friendlier shell: fish

The program that reads what you type is the **shell**.
Ubuntu's is `bash`. We'll use **fish**, which helps you type less.
Ask Claude what `chsh` does, and **predict**
what will change, and when:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y fish
sudo chsh -s /usr/bin/fish $USER
```

(`apt` installs software.)
Close the left pane (`exit`) and open a new one with Alt+Shift+D.
Was your prediction right?

Fish suggests the rest of a command in grey
from what you typed before (→ accepts it),
and Tab finishes names. ↑ brings back earlier commands.

Fish doesn't know yet where Claude was installed. Tell it once:

```fish
fish_add_path ~/.local/bin
```

**Explain** (ask Claude if you're stuck):
what is a "path", and why did bash find Claude but fish didn't?

## An editor: nvim

To write programs we need a text **editor**.
**nvim** runs inside the terminal.

```fish
sudo apt install -y neovim
cd ~/course
nvim hello.txt
```

nvim starts in *normal mode*, where keys are commands, not letters.
Four things are enough:

| Press | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| `i` | start typing (*insert mode*) |
| `Esc` | stop typing |
| `:wq` Enter | save and quit |
| `:q!` Enter | quit *without* saving |

Press `i`, type `hello`, press `Esc`, type `:wq`, press Enter.
**Predict:** what will this print?

```fish
cat hello.txt
```

Stuck in nvim? Press `Esc` a few times, then `:q!`.
(More nvim: type `:Tutor` inside it.)

## Python

```fish
python3
```

The prompt changes to `>>>`: you're talking to Python now.
**Predict** each answer, then check:

```python
2 + 2
7 / 2
7 // 2
2 ** 10
```

Ask Claude why `7 / 2` and `7 // 2` differ,
then explain it back. Leave Python with **Ctrl+D**.

A good place to stop for the day.

# Part 2: Python basics

## Boxes and questions

Start Python again and **predict** each line before pressing Enter:

```fish
python3
```

```python
x = 5
x + 1
x
x = x + 1
x
x == 6
x == 7
```

`x = 5` makes a box called `x` and puts 5 in it.
`x + 1` works out an answer but leaves the box alone.

In maths, `x = x + 1` is nonsense.
In Python, `=` means
**"work out the right side, then put it in the box on the left"**.

`==` *asks* whether two things are equal,
and the answer is `True` or `False`.
One `=` stores, two `==` ask.
Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in programming.

Leave Python with Ctrl+D.

## Decisions: if

```fish
cd ~/course
nvim decide.py
```

Type this in (`i` first, `Esc` and `:wq` at the end):

```python
n = 7
if n % 2 == 0:
    print(n, "is even")
else:
    print(n, "is odd")
```

`%` is the remainder: `7 % 2` is 1.
`if` runs the indented lines under it when its question is `True`,
otherwise the lines under `else:`.
**Predict**, then run:

```fish
python3 decide.py
```

## Indentation: what's inside what

A line ending in `:` starts a **block**:
the lines under it, indented 4 spaces further.
The block ends at the first line that steps back out.
nvim indents for you after a `:`,
but it can't know **when a block ends**.
That's you, pressing Backspace,
and it's a reasoning question: does this line belong inside?

## Repeats: for

```fish
nvim loop.py
```

```python
for k in range(1, 6):
    print(k, k * k)
```

`for` runs the indented line once for each `k` in
`range(1, 6)`: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. It stops *before* 6.
**Predict** all five lines, then run:

```fish
python3 loop.py
```

**Predict** *exactly* what this prints:

```python
for k in range(3):
    if k % 2 == 0:
        print(k, "even")
    else:
        print(k, "odd")
    print("done")
```

How many times does `done` appear?
What changes if `print("done")` moves one step left,
under `for`? Try both and check.

::: {.callout-note}
## Try it yourself
Change `loop.py` to print only the **even** numbers from 1 to 20.
You'll need an `if` inside the `for`.
:::

# Part 3: Adding up

## The story

Around 1785, the story goes,
a teacher told his class to add up every number from 1 to 100.
A ten-year-old, Carl Friedrich Gauss,
wrote the answer almost at once: **5050**.

**How might he have done it?**
Spend two minutes with a pencil before reading on.

## The slow way: a loop

```fish
cd ~/course
nvim gauss.py
```

Type it in yourself (typing teaches more than pasting):

```python
total = 0
for k in range(1, 101):
    total = total + k
    print(k, total)
```

**Predict** the first three lines, then run it:

```fish
python3 gauss.py
```

The last line says `100 5050`.

Now make an error on purpose:
delete the spaces in front of `total = total + k` and run it.
Read the error, guess what it means,
then paste it to Claude with your guess.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why 101?
Change `range(1, 101)` to `range(1, 100)`.
**Predict** the last line, then run it.
An AI makes exactly this kind of mistake,
and you just learned to catch it.
:::

## Gauss's trick

Write the sum forwards and backwards:

```
  1 +  2 +  3 + ... +  99 + 100
100 + 99 + 98 + ... +   2 +   1
```

Each column adds up to **101**, and there are **100** columns.
Two copies of the sum make 100 × 101 = 10100,
so one copy is **5050**. For any $n$:

$$1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$

**Explain it to Claude** in your own words, without the picture,
and let it look for the hole.
(Does your explanation work when $n$ is odd?)

## A check inside the loop

```fish
nvim invariant.py
```

```python
total = 0
for k in range(1, 101):
    total = total + k
    assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
print(total)
```

`assert` means "this must be true here":
if it's false, Python stops with an `AssertionError`.
So this loop checks Gauss's formula after every step.
**Predict**, then run it:

```fish
python3 invariant.py
```

It prints `5050`: no step failed.

Now break the loop on purpose:
change `total + k` to `total + k + 1`.
**Predict:** at which `k` does the `assert` stop it?
Then change it back.

## Check lots of cases

`invariant.py` only checks up to 100.
To check other `n`, we turn the adding-up into a **function**,
made with `def`: a recipe with a name.
[claude: give more defintion of funcitons and def, its an
import basic, and then also introduce what assert does
with perhaps a simpler example to try like assert 4 % 2 == 0
verssu assert 4 % 2 == 1, then after the check, perhaps another one
to do the n^3 example below]

`n` is its input, and `return` hands back the answer,
so `sum_to(100)` is 5050.

```fish
nvim check.py
```

```python
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
    return total

for n in range(1000):
    assert sum_to(n) == n * (n + 1) // 2
print("all 1000 agree")
```

The first part is the loop from `gauss.py`,
indented under `def`, with `n + 1` where 101 was.
The second part asks, for every `n` from 0 to 999,
whether the loop and the formula agree.
**Predict**, then run it:

```fish
python3 check.py
```

It prints `all 1000 agree`.
Is the formula now true for *every* number?
**Decide before reading on.**

No. A thousand examples is still just examples.
Mathematicians have found patterns that held
for millions of cases and then broke.

## Why it can never fail

A claim that stays true after every round
is a **loop invariant**, like the `assert` in `invariant.py`.
Now the big question:
if the `assert` passed in one round,
why *must* it pass in the next?
(What does one round add to `total`?)
**Decide before reading on.**

Say it passed in the round for $k - 1$:

$$2 \cdot \text{total} = (k-1)k$$

The next round, for $k$, adds $k$, so $2 \cdot \text{total}$ grows by $2k$:

$$(k-1)k + 2k = k(k+1)$$

which is exactly what the `assert` checks.
It passes in the first round,
and each passing round makes the next one pass,
so it can never fail, however far the loop runs.

That's no longer a check. It's a proof for every $n$,
and it's the method from maths class: **induction**.
The first round is the first domino,
and each round knocks over the next.

**Write this proof on paper, in your own words.**
You'll need it in Part 4.

::: {.callout-note}
## Try it yourself
1. Add up the odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … and print the running total
   for the first 10. What pattern do you see? *Why* would it hold?
   (Try drawing it with dots.)
2. Ask Claude: *"Write a short Python function that adds up 1 to n,
   with one hidden bug. Don't tell me where."*
   Find the bug by reasoning first, then prove it with a check.
:::

# Part 4: Lean

## Why AI and Lean belong together

A proof that *sounds* right can still be wrong,
and Claude is very good at sounding right.
Lean doesn't care how convincing a proof sounds:
it checks every step, or it refuses.
So the AI suggests, and Lean checks.

That leaves you the most important job:
**does the claim say what you meant?**
Lean checks that the proof proves the claim,
not that it's the claim you wanted.

## What Lean is

Lean is another programming language.
It has boxes and loops, like Python,
and it can also check proofs.
Seeing the same program in a second language
shows which parts are the *ideas* (a box, a repeat)
and which are just *spelling*.

We'll use Lean in the browser, with Claude beside it.
**Claude in Chrome** is Claude in a side panel of Chrome
that can read the page you're on and type into it.
Install the **Claude** extension from the Chrome Web Store,
sign in, and pin it (the puzzle-piece icon, then the pin).

Open [live.lean-lang.org](https://live.lean-lang.org),
delete what's there, and paste:

```lean
def sumLoop (n : Nat) : Nat := Id.run do
  let mut total := 0
  for k in [1:n+1] do
    total := total + k
  return total

#eval sumLoop 100
```

The panel on the right shows `5050`.
Here it is next to `sum_to` from `check.py`:

| Python | Lean |
|--------|------|
| `def sum_to(n):` | `def sumLoop (n : Nat) : Nat :=` |
| `total = 0` | `let mut total := 0` |
| `for k in range(1, n + 1):` | `for k in [1:n+1] do` |
| `total = total + k` | `total := total + k` |
| `return total` | `return total` |

- `Nat` is a **natural number** (0, 1, 2, …).
  `(n : Nat) : Nat` says `n` is one, and so is the answer.
- `let mut` makes a box you can change (*mutable*).
- `:=` puts something into a box, like Python's `=`.
- `Id.run do` says "steps, done in order". Just copy it.
- `#eval` runs a line and shows the answer.

**Explain:** what does Lean make you say that Python doesn't?

## Two programs, one answer

Gauss's formula is a program too, a much faster one.
Add it below:

```lean
def sumFormula (n : Nat) : Nat := n * (n + 1) / 2

#eval sumFormula 100
```

`/` on natural numbers rounds down, like Python's `//`.
(Why doesn't that rounding ever change the answer here?)

## Checking isn't proving

Do the two programs agree? Add one check, for $n = 1000$:

```lean
#eval sumLoop 1000 == sumFormula 1000
```

It shows `true`. Now add the claim for *every* $n$:

```lean
theorem agree (n : Nat) : sumLoop n = sumFormula n := by
  sorry
```

Read it out loud:
"a claim called `agree`: for any natural number $n$,
the loop and the formula give the same answer. Proof: `sorry`."
This is `check.py` again,
for every $n$ instead of a thousand.

`sorry` means "I'll prove this later".
Lean understands the claim but warns:
`` declaration uses `sorry` ``. You still owe a proof,
and checks like `true` don't count.
What Lean wants is an argument like your loop invariant.

## AI translates, Lean checks

Writing Lean proofs yourself comes later in the course.
Today Claude only *translates* your proof,
and you watch what Lean says.

Open Claude in Chrome on the Lean page,
type in your paper proof from Part 3, and ask:

> Please prove `agree` in Lean by translating my proof,
> and see whether Lean accepts it.
> Don't fix any mistakes in my proof,
> and don't fix anything Lean complains about.
> Only translate my proof into Lean,
> and translate Lean's answer back into English.

It may take a few minutes, and then Lean should accept it.
Claude may add a smaller claim along the way
(something like "one more round adds $n + 1$").
**Where is that step in your paper proof?

Next, a claim of my own. Before you send it,
**predict**: is it true? Try $n = 0$, 1 and 2 on paper.
Then ask:

> Now I want to check whether this also means that
> sum(n)^2 = n^3.
> Please convert that to Lean, have Lean check it,
> and translate only Lean's answer back into English.
> Don't fix the proof.

What did Lean say?
And did Claude do only what you asked,
or did it quietly change the claim to one that works?

## What we did today

- Set up Linux with Claude as a tutor, plus fish, nvim and Python.
- Added 1 to 100 with a loop and with Gauss's trick.
- Checked a thousand cases, and saw why that isn't a proof.
- Put a check inside the loop, and saw why it can never fail:
  induction.
- Wrote the same loop in Lean, next to Gauss's formula,
  and claimed the two programs always agree.
- Had Claude translate your proof for Lean to check.

The computer did the adding.
You did the reasoning.
